query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating in‐situ high‐temperature neutron imaging with advanced CALPHAD (third‐generation thermodynamic modeling) can provide accurate and efficient determination of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and other liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast or additively manufactured high‐entropy alloy specimens (e.g., equiatomic or near‐equiatomic systems such as CoCrCuNi or similar compositions) in their solid, metastable state.
generation.intervention: Heat the HEA samples in a controlled high-temperature furnace while performing simultaneous neutron imaging and calorimetric measurements, then calibrate and validate the observations with CALPHAD-derived thermodynamic predictions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in high-temperature furnaces with controlled atmospheres (to avoid oxidation) over a temperature range covering below and above the melting point (e.g., 1000 °C to 1500 °C), ensuring real-time monitoring during heating and cooling cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: The real-time observation of liquid phase behavior—such as phase remixing, volume changes, and onset of melting—correlates directly with structural changes at the atomic level influencing fusion thermodynamics.
generation.mechanism: Neutron imaging captures the dynamics of melting, phase separation or remixing, and volume change, while simultaneously the energy absorbed or released is recorded via calorimetry. The integration of these measurements with a refined CALPHAD model (using third-generation descriptions) reduces uncertainty in evaluating enthalpy, entropy, and volumetric changes associated with fusion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion properties (melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change) predicted by the CALPHAD model will closely match the experimentally measured values (within about 5–10% deviation), indicating both high accuracy and efficiency over conventional ex situ methods.
generation.baseline: Traditional approaches using separate calorimetry and post-mortem structural analysis, which require more time and often involve greater uncertainty due to phase separation or metastability issues.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be most effective for single-phase or compositionally homogeneous HEA melts. In systems with extensive liquid-phase immiscibility or where rapid phase kinetics obscure imaging, the method may face limitations.
generation.uncertainty: While the combined method is predicted to improve accuracy and efficiency, the precise quantitative improvements and the sensitivity to rapid transient phases remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of experiments on a set of HEA samples by performing synchronized in-situ neutron imaging and differential scanning calorimetry during controlled heating and cooling cycles. Calibrate the resulting thermodynamic data using advanced CALPHAD modeling. Then, compare the experimental measurements (melting temperature, measured latent heat, and volume change) with the model predictions across multiple alloy compositions.
measurements: Neutron radiographic time series to track liquid-phase formation and volume changes
Differential scanning calorimetry data for enthalpy and derived entropy of fusion
Temperature profiles during heating and cooling cycles
Comparative analysis with CALPHAD model predictions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, for a significant subset of compositions, the experimental measurements of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change consistently deviate by more than approximately 10% from the CALPHAD predictions, or if the in-situ imaging fails to capture the expected phase behavior correlated to the fusion process, then the integrated approach would be considered falsified.

In-Situ Imaging of Molten High-Entropy Alloys Using Cold Neutrons

Abstract: AbstractReal-time neutron imaging was utilized to produce a movie-like series of radiographs for in-situ observation of the remixing of liquid state immiscibility that occurs in equiatomic CoCrCu with the addition of Ni. A previous neutron imaging study demonstrated that liquid state immiscibility can be observed in-situ for the equiatomic CoCrCu alloy. In this follow-up study, equiatomic buttons of CoCrCu were placed alongside small Ni buttons inside an alumina crucible in a high-temperature vacuum furnace. The mass of the Ni buttons was specifically selected such that when melted in the same crucible as the CoCrCu buttons, the overall composition would become equiatomic CoCrCuNi. Neutron imaging was simultaneously carried out to capture 10 radiographs in 20 °C steps from 1000 °C to 1500 °C and back down to 1000 °C. This, in turn, produced a movie-like series of radiographs that allow for the observation of the buttons melting, the transition from immiscible to miscible as Ni is alloyed into the CoCrCu system, and solidification. Third-Generation Thermodynamic Descriptions for Ta-Cr and Ta-V Binary Systems

Abstract: AbstractThe third-generation thermodynamic descriptions for Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were performed to construct the reliable thermodynamic database for refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) containing Laves phase. The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both solid and liquid phases were established, from which the thermodynamic properties and thermal vacancy can be well described. The thermodynamic descriptions of Ta-Cr and Ta-V over the whole composition and temperature regions were carried out based on the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) approach. Specifically, the thermodynamic parameters of C14 and C15 Laves phases were evaluated by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as the semiempirical relations.
